The takeaway

Your prompts use little water. Where data centers are built matters more.

Seven in ten new data centers are planned in basins where 40% or more of the available water is already withdrawn, nearly the same share as the ones already running. More than one in five also sit where drought keeps coming back. Most local policy actions never mention water.

How we count. “New” means planned or under construction. Data center records: dcmap.us, October 2026 (5,098 U.S. records; 5,042 in the lower 48). Water stress: WRI Aqueduct 4.0 baseline water stress; each record takes the highest rating within 30 miles. “High” means 40–80% of the available water is withdrawn each year, “extremely high” more than 80%. Records with no WRI data (Alaska, Hawaii) are left out of shares. Drought: U.S. Drought Monitor, moderate drought or worse in more than 25% of weeks (2016–2025 and 2021–2025). Policy: Bommarito dataset. A record “mentions water” if its text contains the word; “water standard” records were coded by the authors. Your AI water: a typical value for the range you picked (3, 13, 35, 100, 500, 3,000 or 15,000 prompts a day) × 365 × 0.26 mL, Google’s median for a Gemini text prompt, on-site cooling water only. “Counting electricity” adds 0.24 Wh per prompt × 4.52 L per kWh, the U.S. average from the LBNL report. Your share: LBNL’s 66 billion L (on site) and about 800 billion L (electricity) for 2023, divided by the 2023 U.S. population. Limits. A record counts once whatever its size or cooling system, so these shares show where sites are, not how much water each uses. Planned projects may never be built. Water stress is measured for the basin, not the facility’s actual water source. Company per-prompt figures are self-reported. “Your share” divides the national total evenly by population; data centers also serve businesses and users abroad. The state labels use our own cut-offs: very high water pressure = at least half of new records face both stress and drought; high = at least 70% in high stress; some = at least 30%.
Go deeper · the data

Why water, and why where?

Data center water use is usually reported as one national number. But water runs out basin by basin. We mapped every U.S. data center record against water stress, ten years of drought and local rules. Each card opens that layer on the map.

About

Why we made this

National estimates say U.S. data centers consumed 66 billion liters of water on site in 2023. That number hides the question that matters to the people living next to them: whose water, and how much is left?

Thirst Check is the interactive companion to our short film, The Thirst Behind the Data Center Boom. It starts from the state you live in, then zooms out to the whole country, so the same data can answer a personal question and show the national pattern.

We began with the United States because its data is public and detailed: facility records, basin-level water stress, ten years of weekly drought maps and local policy records. As comparable data becomes available for other countries, the same test and map can grow with it.

Problem

Water is local

Data center water use is reported as national totals, but scarcity is felt basin by basin.

Approach

Overlay the places

Map every record against water stress and a decade of drought, then read local rules for water.

Position

Ask what places can sustain

Seven in ten sites, old and new, sit in stressed basins while most policy actions stay silent on water.
